title: SupplementManifest
description: What supplementary material exists for ONE paper, where it is on disk, and what each part of it contains. A fetch cache plus a content index: the fetch half records how each file arrived (including by hand), the index half names the tables worth reading and their columns, so a later reader can go straight to a sheet instead of re-scanning heterogeneous files. Not curated config — never merge this into cas.json.

manifest_version.description: Bumped when the manifest shape changes in a way that invalidates existing stores.

indexed_at.description: ISO-8601 UTC timestamp of the last time the content index below was (re)written.

files.description: Every supplementary file known for this paper, whether or not it was retrieved. One entry per file as the publisher packages it; members of an archive are listed in `members`, not here.

tables.description: The content index: tables worth reading, wherever they live (a sheet in a workbook, a CSV inside a zip, a table in a document). This is what downstream steps consult to decide what to open.

gaps.description: Things the indexer could not do, stated explicitly so an absence is never mistaken for a negative result. Read this before concluding a paper has no marker tables.

Paper.description: Which paper this manifest belongs to. `doi` is the store key.

role.description: What this paper is relative to the corpus. Mirrors evidence_summary.schema.json's `role`.

access.description: Whether the supplements are reachable programmatically. 'closed' means retrieval is out of scope and files must be supplied by hand.

SupplementFile.description: One supplementary file as the publisher packages it, plus how (or whether) we got hold of it.

file_id.description: Stable id for cross-referencing from TablePointer. The publisher's filename, e.g. '41586_2024_8002_MOESM4_ESM.zip'.

label.description: The publisher's label, verbatim, e.g. 'Supplementary Tables'. From JATS <supplementary-material><label>.

caption.description: The publisher's caption, verbatim, e.g. 'Supplementary Tables 1-40.'. From JATS <caption>. Often the cheapest description of the contents there is — read this before opening anything.

media_type.description: Extension-derived kind: xlsx, csv, tsv, docx, pdf, zip, txt, video, image, other.

path.description: Path to the file on disk, relative to the store root. Absent when status is not 'present'.

status.description: 'present' = on disk. 'listed' = we know it exists but have not fetched it. 'skipped' = deliberately not fetched (see retrieval.note — usually a size cap or a video). 'unavailable' = no route exists (closed access, needs a manual drop). 'failed' = a route was tried and errored.

members.description: For archives: the unpacked member tree. Paths are relative to the archive root and are what TablePointer.member_path refers to.

Retrieval.description: How this file arrived. A file dropped in by hand is a first-class route, not a failure — it is the only route for closed-access papers.

route.description: 'jats_listing' = known from the article XML but bytes not fetched by this route. 'publisher_direct' = fetched from the publisher's static host. 'europepmc_bundle' = from Europe PMC's supplementaryFiles zip. 'manual' = supplied by a user. 'none' = no route available.

sha256.description: Digest of the file as stored, so a re-index can tell whether the bytes changed.

note.description: Why a route was skipped or how it failed. Free text.

path.description: Where the member was unpacked to, relative to the store root. Absent if it was not unpacked.

TablePointer.description: A table worth reading, located precisely enough to slice without searching. Describes the table and its columns; it deliberately does NOT enumerate which cell types appear (that is the reader's job at query time).

file_id.description: The SupplementFile.file_id this table lives in.

member_path.description: Path within the archive, when file_id names an archive.

locator.description: Where in the file: a worksheet name for xlsx, a page number for pdf, a heading for docx. Omit for a single-table file such as a CSV.

table_label.description: The authors' own name for it, verbatim where one exists, e.g. 'Supplementary Table 12'.

content_type.description: What kind of table this is. 'legend' is the manifest/contents sheet that describes the others — worth reading first.

description.description: What the table contains and what a reader would use it for. One or two sentences, grounded in the caption, the legend sheet, or the headers actually seen.

columns.description: The table's columns in order, each with what it holds. The point of the manifest: a reader picks a table by its columns without opening it. For a very wide table (one column per cell state, say) this may be a prefix — compare its length against n_columns.

n_columns.description: Total columns in the table. Greater than the length of `columns` when that list is a prefix of a very wide table.

header_row.description: 0-based index of the header row, so a reader can slice correctly. Publisher tables often carry title rows above the header.

n_rows.description: Data rows excluding the header, where known.

evidence.description: What this characterisation was based on: 'caption', 'legend_sheet', 'headers', or 'rows_read'. Distinguishes a table described from its caption from one actually opened.

description.description: What the column holds, where the header alone is not self-explanatory.

Gap.description: Something the indexer could not do. Keeps 'we did not look' distinguishable from 'there is nothing there'.

reason.description: Why it could not be characterised, e.g. 'archive member exceeds size cap', 'scanned PDF, no extractable text', 'no route to fetch (closed access)'.

action.description: What a human could do about it, e.g. 'drop the file into incoming/'. Omit if nothing would help.
